# `third-party/bt` — fork patches

This file tracks **every** modification made to the vendored `bt` sources. The baseline import is
upstream `com.github.atomashpolskiy:bt` **1.10**, taken from the published `-sources.jar` files and
imported byte-for-byte unmodified (verified by hash comparison against the Gradle-cached jars; see
`NOTICE` for provenance and licensing).

## Fork layout (not a source patch)

- `bt-bencoding` + `bt-core` are vendored as Gradle `java-library` subprojects (`org.blaze:bt-*:1.10-blaze`);
  Java packages stay `bt.*` so the fork is a drop-in replacement.
- `bt-dht` and `bt-http-tracker-client` remain upstream Maven artifacts with the upstream
  `bt-core`/`bt-bencoding` transitively excluded, so only the fork is on the classpath. Rationale in `NOTICE`.
- Build files under `third-party/bt/*/build.gradle.kts` are new blaze-dm scaffolding, not upstream changes.

Connection handling unchanged — the socket is already shut down by `SocketChannelHandler.read` before the loop sees the exception. | TOR-12: real-swarm runs (2026-10-15, nyaa) flooded logs with `Failed to process key` traces while downloads completed correctly; routine hostile/legacy-peer churn must not read like an internal defect. | `bt/net/ReadLoopFailures.java` (new), `bt/net/DataReceivingLoop.java`, `bt-core/build.gradle.kts` (JUnit 4 test scaffolding), `bt/net/ReadLoopFailuresTest.java` (new) | Yes — small, behavior-preserving; matches upstream's own TODO-level noise complaints. |
| 2 | this commit | Extend the #1 classifier with `CONNECTION_CHURN`: `SocketException` (reset/aborted), `EOFException`, `ClosedChannelException` anywhere in the cause chain → DEBUG one-liner; the loop's separate `EOFException` catch collapses into the same switch. Peer misbehavior keeps priority; other I/O failures stay ERROR+trace (conservative). | TOR-12: `Connection reset` from rate-limited/firewalled peers is normal public-swarm churn, previously ERROR+trace (`DataReceivingLoop.java:130-132` upstream). | `bt/net/ReadLoopFailures.java`, `bt/net/DataReceivingLoop.java`, `bt/net/ReadLoopFailuresTest.java` (+5 churn cases) | Yes — same rationale as #1. |
| 3 | this commit | Dependency bump: guava `30.1-jre` → `33.4.8-jre` in `bt-bencoding` (no source change). | 30.1's `AbstractFuture` calls the terminally-deprecated `sun.misc.Unsafe::objectFieldOffset`, spamming a JDK-24+ WARNING on every startup (observed in a real `:gui:run` torrent download). Measured with a SettableFuture probe on JBR 25: 30.1 reproduces the warning, 33.4.8 prints none. Guice 5.0.1 + all engine/fork tests green on the new version. | `bt-bencoding/build.gradle.kts` | Yes — trivial version bump; upstream already allows newer guava at runtime. |
| 4 | this commit | Fast resume (TOR-1): persist the verified-piece bitfield + per-file size/mtime fingerprints on clean session close and trust them — after a fingerprint gate and a configurable random spot-check — instead of re-hashing every byte on each restart. New opt-in machinery: `bt.data.resume` package (`ResumeStore` pluggable interface, `FileResumeStore`, `FastResumeVerifier` decorator); `ChunkVerifier` gains default context method `verify(chunks, bitfield, torrent, storage)` + `onTorrentClosed(...)` hook (defaults preserve old behavior exactly); `Storage.locationOf(...)` default method + `FileSystemStorage` implementation; `DefaultDataDescriptor` calls the context verify (:166) and the close hook in `close()`; `DefaultChunkVerifier.verifyChunks` skips already-verified chunks (no-op when the bitfield starts empty, as in every existing flow); `Config` gains `autoResumeEnabled`/`resumeDirectory`/`resumeSpotCheckCount` (default OFF); `ServiceModule.provideVerifier` decorates only when explicitly enabled. | TOR-1: a multi-hundred-MiB restart re-hashed 100% of data every time (`DefaultChunkVerifier.java:101-108` upstream hashed all chunks regardless of existing bits). Stale/crashed state can never be trusted silently: the save runs only on clean close, every rejection path falls back to the exact full re-hash. | `bt/data/resume/{ResumeStore,ResumeState,FileFingerprint,FileResumeStore,FastResumeVerifier}.java` (new), `bt/data/{Storage,ChunkVerifier,DefaultChunkVerifier,DefaultDataDescriptor}.java`, `bt/data/file/FileSystemStorage.java`, `bt/runtime/Config.java`, `bt/module/ServiceModule.java`, tests: `bt/data/resume/{FastResumeVerifierTest,FileResumeStoreTest}.java`, `bt/data/file/FileSystemStorageLocationTest.java` (22 new cases); engine: `TorrentFastResumeTest` (5 real-swarm integration cases) + `TorrentFastResumeBenchmark` (320 MiB restart numbers) | Yes — self-contained, strictly opt-in; matches the shape qBittorrent/Deluge use for resume data. |
| 5 | this commit | Preallocation (TOR-2): `FileSystemStorage` gains an opt-in `PreallocationMode` constructor overload; new shared `bt.data.file.Preallocation` utility sizes each torrent file to its full length when a unit is created — `NONE` (default) keeps the historical grow-on-write behavior, `SPARSE` extends via a single trailing-byte write (hole body), `FULL` zero-fills only the missing tail preserving existing bytes. All modes idempotent: a file already at target size is not re-touched (bytes *and* mtime — keeps PATCH-4 resume fingerprints valid across restarts). SPARSE and FULL check `FileStore.getUsableSpace` before creating anything and throw `bt.data.InsufficientStorageException` (new). | TOR-2: the torrent path reserved nothing up front and discovered a full disk mid-transfer; HTTP already preallocates (`DefaultFileStorage.kt:47`), this gives the torrent path the same guarantee plus a fail-fast verdict, with NTFS-vs-ext4/APFS charging differences documented in `PreallocationMode`. | `bt/data/{PreallocationMode,InsufficientStorageException}.java` (new), `bt/data/file/{Preallocation,FileSystemStorage}.java`, test: `bt/data/file/PreallocationTest.java` (new, 9 cases); engine: `TorrentContentStorage` preallocation param + `toForkMode()`, `TorrentNetworkClient` preallocation ctor param + `toTorrentDownloadError` cause-chain mapping to `DiskFull`, `DownloadSettings.torrentPreallocation` (default NONE), `TorrentPreallocationTest` (11 cases) | Yes — additive, default-off; upstream issues already ask for preallocation-style control on file storage. |
| 6 | this commit | Web-seed metadata parsing (TOR-3 part 1): `MetadataConstants` gains `WEB_SEED_LIST_KEY` (`url-list`, BEP-19) and `HTTP_SEED_KEY` (`httpseeds`, BEP-17); `Torrent` gains `default` accessors `getWebSeedUrls()`/`getHttpSeedUrls()` (default methods so existing/anonymous implementers keep compiling), implemented on `DefaultTorrent` (unmodifiable lists, empty by default); `MetadataService.buildTorrent` extracts both, preferring the info-dict `url-list` over the root copy (the info-dict form is covered by the info hash) and tolerating a bare-string list. | TOR-3: upstream 1.10 never reads `url-list`/`httpseeds` (`MetadataService.buildTorrent` parses announce/announce-list/info only), so web seeds were invisible to the client. This is the read-only groundwork; the fetch agent is patch #7. | `bt/metainfo/{MetadataConstants,Torrent,DefaultTorrent,MetadataService}.java`, test: `bt/metainfo/WebSeedParsingTest.java` (new, 5 cases) | Yes — purely additive; the default-method accessors leave the existing contract untouched. |
| 7 | this commit | Web-seed transport seam (TOR-3 part 2): new `bt.torrent.webseed` package. `WebSeedPlanner` maps a piece index onto the ordered `WebSeedSegment`s (file index, path, file-relative inclusive byte range) that cover it over the concatenated-file stream — splitting pieces that straddle a file boundary, clipping the short final piece, and skipping zero-length files; plus `pieceCount`/`pieceLength` helpers. `WebSeedFetcher` is the HTTP-agnostic transport interface (`fetch(seedUrl, segment)`) the host application implements, so the fork keeps zero dependency on any HTTP client. | TOR-3: web seeds are plain HTTP file servers addressed by path + `Range` (BEP-17 `httpseeds` and the universally-compatible subset of BEP-19 `url-list`); the correctness-critical piece→file-range math is torrent-structure logic that belongs with the library and is unit-testable without any transport. The download agent + HTTP impl land in the engine. | `bt/torrent/webseed/{WebSeedSegment,WebSeedPlanner,WebSeedFetcher}.java` (new), test: `bt/torrent/webseed/WebSeedPlannerTest.java` (new, 6 cases) | Yes — new, self-contained package; nothing existing changes. |
| 8 | this commit | Adaptive request depth (TOR-5): new `bt.torrent.messaging.RequestWindow` — a per-connection bound on outstanding block requests derived from the measured bandwidth-delay product. It doubles in slow start while the window itself is the bottleneck, then tracks `ceil(throughput × RTT / blockSize)` with additive-increase/decrease toward the target, always bounded by `[minDepth, maxDepth]`; RTT comes from request-issue → block-arrival latency, throughput from delivered-byte deltas sampled once per processing cycle. `ConnectionState` holds the window (package-private, null when disabled); `RequestProducer` now takes `Config`, records issue times, samples a cycle, and gates its drain loop by `window.depth()` instead of the fixed value; `PieceConsumer.checkBlockIsExpected` folds the arrival latency; `InitializeTorrentProcessingStage` passes `config`; `Config` gains `adaptiveRequestDepthEnabled` (default OFF) + `minRequestDepth` (default 8). With adaptive OFF the code path is byte-for-byte the upstream fixed-250 behavior and no window object is allocated. | TOR-5: `maxOutstandingRequests` was one fixed value for every peer (`Config.java:113` default 250, consumed at `RequestProducer.java:105`), wrong in both directions — under-fills a fast low-latency pipe and over-queues a slow high-latency one. Implemented and measured, but kept opt-in: the only controlled instrument (the loopback latency/throttle proxy in `RequestDepthBenchmark`) shows fixed ≥ adaptive, so the production default stays 250 (see `TorrentRuntimeProvider`). | `bt/torrent/messaging/{RequestWindow,RequestProducer,PieceConsumer,ConnectionState}.java`, `bt/processor/torrent/InitializeTorrentProcessingStage.java`, `bt/runtime/Config.java`, test: `bt/torrent/messaging/RequestWindowTest.java` (new, 8 cases); engine: `TorrentRuntimeProvider` (documents the opt-in decision), `TorrentPerformanceConfigTest` (+1), `support/LatencyProxy.kt` (new relay), `AdaptiveRequestDepthTest` (real transfer over ~50 ms RTT + 3 MiB/s cap), `RequestDepthBenchmark` (fixed-vs-adaptive before/after) | Partly — the BDP window is general and upstreamable; enabling it in Blaze's perf config is a project policy call. |
| 9 | this commit | Synchronous session-finalize completion signal (TOR-7): `TorrentRegistry` gains two default methods — `beginSession(TorrentId)` (no-op by default) and `finalizeSession(TorrentId): Boolean` (returns `false` by default, so a non-supporting registry degrades to the host's old polling). `AdhocTorrentRegistry` implements them: `finalizeSession` takes a striped lock (64 `ReentrantLock`s keyed by `Math.floorMod(torrentId.hashCode(), 64)`), marks the id *finalizing*, fires `EventSink.fireTorrentStopped(id)` (the `EventBus` delivers synchronously in the caller thread — `AdhocTorrentRegistry.onTorrentStopped` unregisters + closes the data descriptor inline), then returns `true` only once the descriptor and id are provably gone. `beginSession` lifts the guard. Both `register(...)` overloads are gated by the same stripe: while an id is finalizing, a late `register` throws `IllegalStateException("Torrent session is being finalized: …")` instead of re-inserting a descriptor that would poison the next real session. Fresh-session-only hooks clear the guard: `DefaultClient.doStartAsync` calls `beginSession` for magnet ids (id known from btih), and `FetchTorrentStage.doExecute` — the first point a file/URL session learns its id — calls it for file/URL (a dying file session has already passed this stage before its metadata event could reach the caller, so it never re-clears). | TOR-7: the engine's `awaitTorrentSettled` polled the registry with `Thread.sleep` (250 ms natural-settle + 100 ms hold, up to 4 rounds ≈ ~350 ms floor) because `DefaultClient.stop()` returns void with no completion future, and that latency is paid on the scheduler's **global queue mutex** — laggy pause for every download. With a real completion signal the poll is gone: idle-pause teardown measured at ~1.7 ms (budget 200 ms) in `TorrentPauseResumeTest`, and the "Torrent already registered" resume race stays closed by the guard. Kept the bounded poll as the engine's slow-path safety net for a session that never reaches the fast path. | `bt/torrent/{TorrentRegistry,AdhocTorrentRegistry}.java`, `bt/DefaultClient.java`, `bt/processor/torrent/FetchTorrentStage.java`, `bt/processor/TorrentProcessorFactory.java` (pass the registry to the stage), test: `bt/torrent/AdhocTorrentRegistryFinalizeTest.java` (new, 5 cases: synchronous removal, late-register rejection, beginSession resume, never-registered id, idempotency); engine: `TorrentNetworkClient.awaitTorrentSettled` fast path, `TorrentPauseResumeTest` teardown budget | Yes — additive default methods; the guard only engages for a registry that opts in, and mirrors the deterministic teardown qBittorrent/libtorrent expose. |

Append one row per patch commit. Each patch gets its own commit with a message scoped
`fix(third-party/bt): …` / `feat(third-party/bt): …`, and MUST be accompanied by a test in
`download-engine` (or a `third-party/bt` module test) demonstrating the behavior.
